Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT or THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT Francisco Oold Condominium II, EDSA cor. Mapagmahal St. Diliman. Quezon City OF THE SEQETARY Nn 14 S. 7 February 14, 2007 MAYOR SERGIO G. AMORA, JR. Candijay, Bohol Dear Mayor This is in response to your letter-query seeking the opinion of this Department on issues relative to the authority of the local chief executive to negotiate, enter into and sign a loan contract with a banking institution in order to finance a local project. Based on the information and documents fumished us, the Sangguniang Bayan of Candijay, Bohol, approved on January 13, 2006 Resolution No. 2006-1-2, authorizing and giving full power to you as the Municipal Mayor to negotiate, enter into sign a loan contract with the Land Bank of the Philippines (LBP) in the amount of PO million for the purchase of specified heavy equipments, subject to the ratification by the Bayan. The amount of loan will be secured by IRA/income of the local govemmefft unit. Pursuant to the said Resolution, you applied for loan with the LBP after the winning bidder to supply the heavy equipments was duly determined in a bidding conducted for the purpose. Ihe loan was approved by the LBP but the release of the proceeds thereof was withheld because the bank required a ratification by the Sangguniang Bayan in view of the provision in the aforesaid Resolution which reads "subject to ratification by the SB". You now seek our opinion on whether or not the said ratification is, indeed, required under the law. Before answering your query, it is worth revisiäng the following provisions Of KA 7160 or the Local Government Code Of 1991, to wit: "Section 297. (a) A local government unit may contract loans, credits and other forms of indebtedness with any government or domestic private bank and other lending institutions to finance the construction, installation, improvement, expansion, operation, or maintenance of public faciliües, infrastructure facilities, housing projects, the acquisition of real property, and the implementation of other capital invesünent projects, subject to such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon by the local government unit and the lender. The proceeds from such transactions shall accrue directly to the local government unit concerned." "Section 22. (c) Unless otherwise provided in this Code, no contract may be entered into by the local chief executive in behalf of the local

.2- government unit without prior authorization by the sanggunian concerned." "Section 444. (b) For efficient, effecnve and economical governance the purpose of which is the general welfare of the municipality and its inhabitants pursuant to Section 16 of this Code, the municipal mayor shall: (vi) Upon authorization by the sangguniang bayan, represent the municipality in all its business transactions and sign on its behalf all bonds, contracts, and obligations, and such other documents made pursuant to law or ordinance." "Section 447. (a) (2) (iü) Subject to the provisions of Book II of this Code and upon the majority vote of all the members of the sangguniang bayan, authorize the municipal mayor to negotiate and contract loans and other forms of indebtedness." Based on the foregoing, it is clear and unequivocal that a. Local Qovemment Unit (LOU), through the Local Chief Executive concerned, may contract loans to finance, among others, infrastructure facilities, upon prior authorization by the sanggunian concemed. In our earlier DILG Opinion No. 48, s. 1996, the Department opined that the phrase "upon authority of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan" (Sangguniang bayan in your case) refers to prior authorization given by the before the Local Chief Executive (LCD) could enter into a contract in behalf of the LOU. That authority should not be confused with "pre-approval" of contracts. It is worth that the Local Qovemment Code did not vest unto the Sanggunian the power or authority to pre-approve after it has already given its prior authorization to the LCE to enter into said contract. 'Ihe authority of the is simply limited to the grant of prior authorization of the LCE before entering into any contract. The reason for this could have been obvious, i.e. separation of powers. It is settled that the LCE performs executive functions while the Sangguniang Bayan, of which the Vice Mayor is also a component member, performs legislative functions. Laws and jurisprudence would tell us that there should be separation of powers and functions between the execuüve and legislative bodies, and that encroachment in either is not countenanced. Pre-approval of a contract or ratification of a contract by the Sang;unian after it has already given its prior authorization to the LCE to enter into a contract and the latter has, in fact, already entered into the contract, can be readily construed and viewed as an encroachment of the executive prerogative of the LCE. We are of the view that once the authorization has been given by the Sanggunian, it becomes now the responsibility and power of the LCE, pursuant to his executive power, to operationalize the authority previously given by now entering into the contract. All inadequacies and illegalities that may attend in the execution of the contract is the sole responsibility of the LCE.

'Ihis would explain why that the Local Government Code does not anymore require that the Sanggunian must also ratify the contract after the LCE and the other contracting party could have entered into the contract. The clear legislative intention is to avoid encroachment into each other's powers and functions, i.e. that of the executive and legislative. Thus, the stipulation found in the Resolution that the contract is subject to the ratification by the Sangguniang Bayan can just be considered as if not written considering that it is a condition viewed as contrary to law and policy. Accordingly, there being already a prior authority to enter into a contract given by the Sanggunian to the LCE, all that is needed is for the I to enter into said contract and it becomes incumbent upon him to ensure that the stipulations therein are all in accordance with law, and that he will execute and implement the same, as an incident of his executive functions, in accordance with laws, rules and regulations relevant thereto. Corollary to the foregoing, the Supreme Court ruling in the case of "Villacorta vs. Bernardo" (143 SCRA 480) is instructive where the court ruled that ordinances providing for additional requirements on top of those already required by law, even if made in the guise of implementing the very same law, is ultra vires. We hope we håve enlightened you on this matter. Legal:28/Merle cc: Director Rene K. Burdeos DILO Regional omce NO. 07 Cebu City Very truly yours, RONALDO . PU 01 OF THE RYLYi"o.
